grammar[1].fact: Germans are often said to be blunt, and in private they are. In writing and in public, they use more hedges than you might expect: *eher*, *durchaus*, *gewissermaßen*. Two in one sentence is polite. Four means you are hiding something.

document.intro: A real plaque at the Hamburger Kunsthalle, in two languages, which makes it a free lesson in how German packs a sentence. Compare *1863–68 errichtet auf der Alsterhöhe* with the English, which needs a whole verb.
document.fact: The German half of this plaque has no finite verb at all, only *errichtet* and a list. The English half needs *was built*. Museums love this style, and you’ll see it on every label from here on.

reading.intro: Lena’s cousin has opened her first exhibition: twelve large grey canvases. Frau Huber has come for the wine. Max has been told to say something nice. He has been studying this chapter, and the artist, Sina, is standing right beside him with hopeful eyes.
reading.photos[1].caption: In einer Ausstellung: Man steht, man nickt, man sagt „interessant“.
reading.fact: In a German review, *interessant* is rarely a compliment, and *ambitioniert* usually means it failed. *Durchaus gelungen* is praise with its hands in its pockets. Critics’ language is a code, and learning it is half of C1.
